title: HUMAN TERRITORIAL FUNCTIONING AT THE SCALE OF RESIDENTIAL ENVIRONMENTS
research_question: How do urban residents perceive, behave and transform their residential environments in the recent era? What is the relationship between territorial functioning and spatial layouts? What are the new forms of territoriality at the age of postmodernity? What is the content and extent of urban resident’s territory? Are we still dependent on space? What is the significance of residential environments in urban resident’s territorial network? Did urban residents lose their territorial associations with their near-home territories or are they still dependent on near-home territories? Is the notion of ‘mahalle’ (neighborhood) disappearing, residential areas becoming solely dormitories? Whether provision of certain services and facilities within a catchment area still valid? How do urban residents perceive / behave in their near-home territory? How do residents perceive their residential territories? Do residents still conceive their residential living spaces as a meaningful territorial unit? How subjective definitions of neighborhood boundaries are constructed and used by residents living in diverse urban fabrics? Can we talk about a consensus about the conception of residential territories among its residents? What parts of the territorial unit are included/excluded in their spatial cognition? What are the impacts of socio-economic and demographic characteristics of residents on the cognition of residential territory or territorial behavior? What aspects of physical environment has an affect on human territorial functioning at the scale of residential living space? What are the impacts of physical characteristics of the surrounding context on territorial functioning? How do different spatial organization of residential areas affect territorial functioning? How the changes in residential developments affected the sense of territoriality? How different territorialities are formed in different residential areas, such as traditional neighborhoods and contemporary ones? Which types of physical environments enhance or weaken residents’ territorial attachment?

participants.description: 300 residents from Kavaklıdere district and 300 residents from Çukurambar district in Ankara, Turkey, aged 18 and above. The sample groups are representative of the residing population in terms of sex, age, and educational levels, and represent a variety of occupational groups.
participants.recruitment: Systematic sampling for households, random opportunity sampling for individual respondents on each street.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Kavaklıdere district (traditional, continuous fabric, middle-class, early-republican era) and Çukurambar district (contemporary, high-rise, gated communities, luxury residential, post-1990s transformation) in Ankara, Turkey.
A3 sized base maps of the respective districts for cognitive mapping exercises, showing street names and a few landmarks for orientation.

measures.instrument: GIS analysis of overlapping cognitive maps
Cognitive mapping (point designation on base map) and open-ended questions

measures.construct: Territorial Cognition: Territorial Gaps (Fear and Discomfort Zones)
measures.instrument: Cognitive mapping (self-drawing on base map) and open-ended questions

measures.construct: Territorial Behavior: Exclusive Use as a Resource Base (Activity Nodes)
measures.instrument: Matrix-type questionnaire on activity types, frequency of use, time interval preferred, mode of transportation, time to reach

measures.construct: Territorial Behavior: Control and Defense (Boundary Markers)
Territorial Behavior: Control and Defense (Central Markers)

measures.instrument: Likert scale (1-5), dichotomous, and open-ended questions
Questionnaire (age, gender, occupation, household type/size, tenure type, length of residence, car ownership, education level)

findings.quote: Kavaklıdere has a more aging population while in Çukurambar the age group between 0-19 is significantly higher

findings.mechanism: Higher amount of new buildings and luxurious/prestigious identity in Çukurambar
findings.quote: housing prices per unit (₺/m²) in Çukurambar is significantly higher (almost double) than in Kavaklıdere

findings.consequent: Number of business owners among respondents
findings.mechanism: Higher number of small-scale businesses located within Kavaklıdere
findings.quote: the number of business owners among the respondents is significantly higher in Kavaklıdere
the number of housewives is higher among the respondents of Çukurambar

findings.mechanism: Kavaklıdere: younger people moving back to city center, smaller units. Çukurambar: higher married couples with children.
findings.quote: The average household size among the respondents is 2,77 in Kavaklıdere and 3,51 in Çukurambar.

findings.mechanism: Kavaklıdere: older population moving to periphery, younger people renting. Çukurambar: transformation from squatter area.
findings.quote: The number of houseowners is significantly higher in Çukurambar, while the lower number of houseowners in Kavaklıdere

findings.mechanism: Kavaklıdere: formed earlier. Çukurambar: transformation from squatter area 1980s-2000s.
findings.quote: majority of the respondents in Çukurambar are living in the same area for 10-20 years while in Kavaklıdere the majority have been living in the area for more than 20 years

findings.mechanism: Socio-economic profile, larger household sizes, higher housing prices in Çukurambar.
findings.quote: the percentage of car ownership is lower among the respondents in Kavaklıdere. Besides, respondents having more than one car is also higher in Çukurambar
majority of the respondents in both cases are very satisfied with their residential area

findings.consequent: Plans to move out from the area
findings.quote: only 22% of the total respondents plan to move to another district in Ankara

findings.mechanism: Women (M=5) significantly higher satisfaction than men (M=4).
findings.quote: The only statistically significant difference between satisfaction levels is of women and men (Mann Whitney U test, p <0.05) in Kavaklıdere.

findings.mechanism: Both: easy access to facilities, environmental quality. Çukurambar: green spaces, access to education. Kavaklıdere: neighbors, access to work.
findings.quote: The most frequently mentioned positive aspects in both districts are the easy access to facilities as well as environmental quality.

findings.mechanism: Both: inadequate parking, noise. Kavaklıdere: lack of green spaces. Çukurambar: environmental pollution (construction sites).
findings.quote: the prominent negative aspects of their residential environments are inadequate parking area and noise.

findings.antecedent: Territorial organization of built environment (Kavaklıdere vs. Çukurambar)
findings.consequent: Proximity, permeability, and delimitation of boundaries
findings.quote: the prominent types of districts diverge in terms of proximity, permeability and delimitation of boundaries on physical, visual and territorial levels

findings.antecedent: Narrower front yards and smaller parcel sizes in Kavaklıdere
findings.quote: In Kavaklıdere, narrower front yards as well as smaller parcel sizes creates smaller semi-private territories

findings.antecedent: Larger front yards and parcels in Çukurambar
findings.quote: in contrast with the larger front yards and parcels in Çukurambar.

findings.antecedent: Hard physical boundary markers (high walls, fences) and long distances between private and public territory in Çukurambar
findings.mechanism: Creates a deaf interface zone between private and public territories.
findings.quote: the larger semi private territories of Çukurambar are both physically and visually impermeable due to hard physical boundary markers

findings.antecedent: Parking areas within front yards of gated communities in Çukurambar
findings.mechanism: Creates a deaf interface zone between private and public spaces.
findings.quote: parking areas within the front yards of gated communities in Çukurambar increases the size of semi-private zones while creating again a deaf interface zone

findings.antecedent: Narrow front yards and sidewalks transformed into parking areas in Kavaklıdere
findings.mechanism: Leaves semi-private zone to cars rather than pedestrians.
findings.quote: the narrow front yards and even sidewalks are transformed into parking areas due to crowding in Kavaklıdere district

findings.antecedent: Front yards with sitting places and softer boundary markers in Kavaklıdere
findings.consequent: Permeability of interface zone between private and public territories
findings.mechanism: Provides for an active and more permeable interface zone.
findings.quote: few examples of front yards with sitting places located in Kavaklıdere district which provides for an active and more permeable interface zone

findings.mechanism: Major streets are conceived as the main boundaries.
findings.quote: the results reveal that major streets are conceived as the main boundaries of the residential territory in both cases

findings.antecedent: Monumental structures (e.g., Kocatepe mosque) or historical sites (e.g., Kuğulupark)
findings.mechanism: Act as boundary mechanisms through marking starting or ending points of residential territory.
findings.quote: a monumental structure acting as a landmark... or a historical site with strong identity... may also orientate residents by acting as boundary mechanisms

findings.consequent: Average size of perceived residential boundaries
findings.mechanism: Kavaklıdere: 60 ha (walking-distance scale). Çukurambar: 90 ha (driving-distance scale).
findings.quote: the average size of the perceived boundaries in Kavaklıdere decreases to 60 ha while it increases to 90 ha in Çukurambar.

findings.mechanism: Access to a larger area with a car.
findings.quote: perceived residential territory size of the respondents who own a car (M = 55.5 ha) is significantly larger than the territory size of the non-car owners (M = 39 ha).

findings.mechanism: Younger and student respondents tend to perceive a block-scale residential area.
findings.quote: the perceived residential territory size of the individuals aged 18-24 (M = 20 ha) are significantly smaller than the size of individuals who are 25-39 (M = 53,0 ha), 40-60 (M = 53 ha) and 60+ (M = 43 ha) years old.

findings.mechanism: Students perceive smaller units, possibly due to higher mobility and use of multiple territories.
findings.quote: the perceived residential territory size of the students (M = 22 ha) are significantly smaller than public employees (M = 53 ha), free lancers (M = 50,5 ha), retired respondents (M = 62 ha) and others (M = 69 ha).

findings.antecedent: Occupation (private sector employees, business owners) in Kavaklıdere
findings.mechanism: Perceive smaller units than retired and other occupational groups.
findings.quote: the perceived residential territory size of private sector employees (M = 39 ha) and business owners (M = 36.5 ha) are also significantly smaller than retired (M = 62 ha) and other (M = 69 ha) occupational groups.

findings.mechanism: Higher number of housewives among women, who use near-home territories more actively.
findings.quote: the size of women's perceived residential territory size (M = 54 ha) is significantly smaller than that of men (M = 74 ha).

findings.antecedent: Education level (literate/secondary school graduates) in Çukurambar
findings.mechanism: Related to university campuses perceived as within residential area by students of higher education.
findings.quote: The perceived residential territory size of the respondents who are literate or secondary school graduates (M = 43 ha) is significantly smaller than the size of the respondents with graduate degrees (M = 101 ha).

findings.mechanism: Higher in Çukurambar (171-210 overlaps) than Kavaklıdere (131-170 overlaps).
findings.quote: consensus on the core area is higher in Çukurambar (overlapping 171 to 210 times among the respondents) than Kavaklıdere (overlapping 131 to 170 times among the respondents).

findings.mechanism: Mainly concentrated along commercial uses.
findings.quote: the shared core is mainly concentrated along commercial uses within the residential territories.

findings.consequent: Types of landmarks mentioned by residents
findings.mechanism: Buildings are most memorable, open spaces least. Çukurambar has more buildings as landmarks due to numerical street names.
findings.quote: majority of the respondents refer to a building and secondly to a street whereas open spaces and areas referring both to a street and an open space are the least mentioned

findings.antecedent: Lack of open spaces with memorable layouts/characteristics
findings.consequent: Open spaces not perceived as landmarks
findings.mechanism: Points to inadequate distribution of open public territories.
findings.quote: the dominance of buildings perceived as landmarks, as well as open spaces such as parks not being perceived as landmarks as well as lack of open public spaces at the shared core area of both districts points out to inadequate distribution of open public territories

findings.consequent: Number of territorial gaps (fear/discomfort zones) demarcated by residents
findings.mechanism: Çukurambar: 113 respondents, Kavaklıdere: 41 respondents.
findings.quote: the number of territorial gaps is low in both cases, there is differentiation between the two districts. In Kavaklıdere, only 41 respondents demarcated an area as fear or discomfort zones among the 300 respondents while in Çukurambar this number increases up to 113.

findings.mechanism: Security emergencies, noise pollution, parking problems, crowding.
findings.quote: The most frequently mentioned territorial gaps in Kavaklıdere are embassies located at the west of the district along Atatürk Boulevard due to security emergencies occurring time to time as well as bars and restaurants along Tunus Avenue which are declared as discomfort zones due to late closing hours creating noise pollution in the area, parking problems for the residents as well as crowding.

findings.antecedent: Vacant lots, construction sites, parks with inadequate lighting/stray dogs in Çukurambar
findings.quote: In Çukurambar, the most frequently mentioned territorial gaps are vacant lots either next to a construction sites or areas on which few squatters are existing. Yet, parks are also referred as discomfort zones due to inadequate lightning and stray dogs.
low positive correlation between total activity and satisfaction scores (r = 0,206; p <0,001) in Çukurambar
low-level positive correlation between the number of landmarks and the perceived residential area size (r = 0,177; p <0,01) in Kavaklıdere

findings.consequent: Functional structure of activity nodes (recreational, commercial)
findings.quote: The functional structure of the activity nodes yields similar results in both districts, predominantly on recreational and commercial purposes

findings.antecedent: Malls located within and near Çukurambar
findings.consequent: Shopping activities (other than grocery) done within residential territory
findings.quote: shopping activities other than daily grocery shopping (clothing, electronics etc.) are done 19 percent more within the residential territory in Çukurambar.

findings.antecedent: Business towers and public institutions in/near Çukurambar
findings.consequent: Use of residential territory for work purposes
findings.quote: The use of residential territory for work purposes is also 19 percent more in Çukurambar

findings.antecedent: Walkable environment (large sidewalks, greenery, active front yards) in Kavaklıdere
findings.mechanism: Increases feeling of security and provides stimulation.
findings.quote: higher amounts of strolling can be associated with the walkability in Kavaklıdere district with larger sidewalks with greenery as well as active front yards both increasing the feeling of security as well as providing stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Larger park areas and higher number of children/married couples with children in Çukurambar
findings.consequent: Open-air sport activities and use of playgrounds
findings.quote: the higher number of open-air sport activities can be related to larger park areas located within the district and more use of playgrounds to the higher number of children between the 0-9 age range in Çukurambar (2304) than Kavaklıdere (1131) as well as to the higher number of married couples with children among the respondents of Çukurambar.

findings.antecedent: Theaters and art galleries in Kavaklıdere
findings.quote: Socio-cultural activities are attended 13 percent more in Kavaklıdere which may be resulting from 2 main theaters (Akün and Şinasi Theaters) as well as many art galleries located in the district.

educational facilities are 14 percent more utilized in Çukurambar which can be associated with the two university campuses (Çankaya and Ufuk Universities) located within the district in addition to one (METU) located at the southern part of the district

findings.consequent: Type and frequency of activities done within residential territory
findings.mechanism: Facilitative impact on overt behavior of residents.
findings.quote: type of activities done and their frequencies within the residential territory is directly affected from the affordances of the environment.

findings.consequent: Prominent mode of transport to reach activities
findings.mechanism: Kavaklıdere: on foot. Çukurambar: by car.
findings.quote: majority of the activities in Kavaklıdere are accessed on foot while in Çukurambar the prominent mode of access is by car.

findings.consequent: Perception and use of residential territory
findings.quote: Çukurambar respondents both perceive and use their residential territory in terms of driving distances

findings.consequent: Perception and corporeal experience of residential environment
findings.quote: in Kavaklıdere the smaller areas perceived as residential territory as well as the prominent type of access to activities on foot refers to perception and corporeal experience of residential environment at a walking distance scale.

findings.antecedent: Territorial organization of space (Çukurambar vs. Kavaklıdere)
findings.mechanism: Çukurambar: less permeable (high walls, fences, locked/automated gates). Kavaklıdere: more permeable (lower walls, iron fences with planting).
findings.quote: the majority of the boundary markers used in Çukurambar are less permeable than Kavaklıdere both physically and visually with higher walls and fences as well as locked or automated gates at the entrances.

findings.mechanism: More common in Çukurambar.
findings.quote: the use of surveillance mechanisms at the boundaries is also more common in Çukurambar.

findings.antecedent: Hard elements as boundary markers in Çukurambar
findings.consequent: Nested character and continuity between territories
findings.mechanism: Destroys nested character and continuity, prohibits social interactions.
findings.quote: the use of hard elements as boundary markers also destroys the nested character and continuity between different territories and when combined with the passive intermediary zones in the district decreases the defensibility of space as discussed by Newman as well as prohibiting social interactions

findings.antecedent: Narrower side-yards between private territories in Kavaklıdere
findings.mechanism: Creates inadequate spacing for privacy due to shorter distances between balconies and windows.
findings.quote: the narrower side-yards between private territories in Kavaklıdere creates shorter distances between balconies and windows of apartment blocks facing each other which creates inadequate spacing for providing privacy

findings.antecedent: Narrower and active front yards with softer boundary markers in Kavaklıdere
findings.mechanism: Through 'eyes on the street'.
findings.quote: narrower and active front yards with softer boundary markers between the private and public territories enhance the defensibility of space through ‘eyes on the street’.

findings.antecedent: Use of central markers in private territory (Kavaklıdere)
findings.consequent: Appropriation of space and sense of territoriality
findings.mechanism: Sitting areas, potted plants, iron gates with ornaments, personalized balconies, name plates.
findings.quote: the use of central markers at the individual scale of the private territory is high and in multiple forms in Kavaklıdere which connotes to the appropriation of space and sense of territoriality at the private scale of the housing plot.

findings.antecedent: Visibility of central markers from adjoining territories (Çukurambar)
findings.consequent: Communication of identity and appropriation of space
findings.mechanism: High fences and walls obstruct visibility.
findings.quote: although there are sitting places and decorations in some of the front-yards they are not visible along the street due to high fences and walls, thus they cannot be regarded as central markers used for territorial claim that radiates outward from the territory.

findings.antecedent: Street art (graffiti, stair coloring, street writings) in Kavaklıdere
findings.consequent: Group identity, spatial attachment, social cohesion at public scale
findings.mechanism: Personalization at the public scale.
findings.quote: various forms of street art can be observed at the public territory in the form of graffiti, stair coloring and street writings in Kavaklıdere... personalization at the public scale that is the existence of central markers can be regarded as a sign of group identity, spatial attachment as well as social cohesion.

findings.antecedent: Scarce public central markers in Çukurambar
findings.consequent: Social cohesion, spatial attachment, group identity
findings.quote: lower number of central markers in Çukurambar at the public scale indicates lower levels of social cohesion, spatial attachment and indication of group identity and belonging.

findings.antecedent: Higher number of central markers (private and public) in Kavaklıdere
findings.consequent: Place attachment and stimulation from environment
findings.quote: the higher number of central markers in Kavaklıdere district both at the individual level of the private territory and collective level of the public territory implies higher degrees of place attachment and stimulation from the surrounding environment at the residential scale.

findings.mechanism: Different designs of the environment reveal different territorialities.
findings.quote: the spatial organization of space is a prominent factor causing the differences in territorial functioning at the residential scale.

findings.antecedent: Loss of intermediary zones (erosion of semi-public domain) in Çukurambar
findings.mechanism: Lack of 'eyes on the street' and narrow sidewalks reduce active use of near home environments.
findings.quote: since there is a lack of defensibility of space, less number of eyes on the street and when combined with the narrow sidewalks decrease the ability of the residents to actively use their near home environments

findings.antecedent: Passive intermediary zones between public and private territories
findings.mechanism: Results in smaller number of central markers.
findings.quote: passive intermediary zones between the public and private territories also decreases the probability of social interaction at this scale which also results in the smaller number of central markers

findings.antecedent: Active or passive character of interface zones and permeability of boundary markers
findings.quote: the active or passive character of these interface zones between the public and private territories and proximity and permeability of boundary markers used in each territory is an important parameter affecting the quality of the lived space.

findings.mechanism: Creates variances in territorial functioning at cognitive and behavioral levels, though less effective than physical context.
findings.quote: societal factors also have a significant impact on human territorial functioning. On the other hand, the findings put forth that societal factors are less effective on territorial functioning than affordances of the environment.

findings.consequent: Exclusive use of residential territory as a resource base
findings.mechanism: Existence of a variety of functions within and at a close proximity to the district has a facilitative impact on behavior.
findings.quote: affordance of the environment is also a prominent determinant of territorial functioning especially in terms of exclusive use of residential territory as a resource base.

findings.antecedent: Services and facilities further away than catchment areas (as proposed in theory)
findings.consequent: Inclusion in residents' cognitive maps as residential territory
findings.mechanism: Buffer zone at the periphery can be an exclusive base for higher needs.
findings.quote: services and facilities that are further away than the catchment areas proposed in theory and practice are included in the resident’s cognitive maps as located within their residential territory and actively used by the respondents.

mechanisms: Territorial functioning links household members to local society and reduces external stressors on household functioning.
Territoriality provides order and predictability, reducing environmental load and stress.
Territoriality facilitates performance of chosen behaviors.
Territoriality promotes personal identity, group identity, and social cohesion.
Territoriality enables predictable and efficient resource distribution.
Territorial functioning reduces conflict through boundary mechanisms and provides desired privacy/publicness.
Physical environment influences territorial functioning, which in turn transforms territorial organization of space (bidirectional relationship).
Cognitive maps (schemata) help individuals process spatial information efficiently and develop adaptive behaviors.
Active front yards with softer boundary markers create active and permeable interface zones, enhancing defensibility through 'eyes on the street'.
Higher number of central markers (personalization) implies higher degrees of place attachment and stimulation.
moderators: Location of the area (inner city, outer city, suburban)
Desirability of goal object (quality/amount of facilities)
implementation_implications: Planning policies should focus on the 'core' areas of neighborhoods rather than solely boundary-defined interventions.
Depiction of territorial gaps provides accurate insights for planning interventions to address dissatisfaction hotspots.
Residential environment designs should consider the catchment area and walking distance neighborhood paradigms, but also acknowledge driving-distance scales for certain populations.
Planning interventions should focus on the absence of public spaces at the shared core of residential environments.
Urban design studies should aim to enhance and enrich the contribution of the built environment on user experience by finding appropriate tools and addressing local issues.

Design should provide desired levels of privacy and publicity with active intermediary zones, used as an exclusive resource base, modified by residents to foster place attachment and a meaningful territorial unit.
Consensus maps provide an alternative method for planning studies by linking tangible and intangible aspects of urban space.

limitations: Territoriality is a multifactorial and intangible phenomenon, making it hard to gauge and interpret.
The research is limited to two case studies, which may limit generalizability.
The study is conducted at a single time section, while environments and human behavior are in constant flux.
